title: In 1980 Mount St. Helens collapsed in the largest landslide on land ever recorded
body: Through late April and early May 1980, magma pushing into Mount St. Helens, in Washington State, made its north flank bulge outwards by 1.5 to 1.8 m a day. At 8:32 a.m. on 18 May, a magnitude 5.1 earthquake right under that slope shook it loose: about **2.9 km³** of rock slid away, the largest landslide on land in recorded history. That suddenly exposed the gas-charged magma inside to much lower pressure, and seconds later it exploded sideways. The blast knocked down about 600 km² of forest and killed about 57 people, and the mountain ended up some 400 m shorter.

cover.alt: False-colour satellite image of forested mountains shown in red, with the white snowy cone of Mount St. Helens before 1980
cover.credit: NASA Goddard Space Flight Center · Public domain

slides.alt: A sequence of false-colour satellite images, one per year: red forest surrounds a small white snowy peak until 1980, when a huge grey scar appears and the peak becomes a crater opening to the north; over the following decades the grey area slowly turns red again.
slides.caption: One Landsat image a year from 1975 to 2025, in false colour: plants show red, ash and bare rock grey. In 1980 the snowy summit becomes a crater, and the flattened forest slowly regrows.
slides.credit: NASA Goddard Space Flight Center, Ross K. Walter (SSAI) · Public domain · excerpt

slides.question: How much forest did the sideways blast knock down?
slides.explanation: About 600 km² (230 square miles) of forest were flattened: the grey scar in the clip. The blast started at about 350 km/h and sped up to around 1,080 km/h.

slides.heading: Height of Mount St. Helens
slides.note: The landslide and blast took about 400 m off the top

slides.heading: Why some slopes regrew faster
slides.text: Where the blast hit open ground head-on, it stripped the soil and delayed new growth for many years. Where it passed overhead, topsoil and seeds survived, and shrubs and other plants came back sooner; some sheltered stands recovered quickly.

slides.question: Before the eruption, how fast was the north flank bulging outwards?
slides.explanation: Magma forcing its way into the volcano pushed the north flank out by 1.5 to 1.8 m a day, until an earthquake shook it loose on 18 May.
